You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Use a French Press: A Step-by-Step Guide to a Clean, Full-Bodied Cup
Meta description: Learn how to use a French press: the right ratio, coarse grind, water temperature, steep time and plunge technique for a clean, full-bodied cup.
Slug: how-to-use-a-french-press

To use a French press, weigh about 1 g of coffee for every 15–16 g of water, grind it coarse, pour water just off the boil, steep for about 4 minutes, skim the crust, then plunge slowly and pour out every drop at once [G]. Get those variables right and you get the heavy, rounded body the method is known for, without a layer of sludge at the bottom of the mug. The rest of this guide covers each step and the reasoning behind it, plus how to keep your press clean.

## Why the French press tastes the way it does

A French press is an immersion brewer. Instead of water flowing through a bed of coffee, as it does in pour-over, all of the grounds sit in all of the water for the whole brew. Extraction is even and forgiving, and it is controlled mostly by grind size and time.

The other half of the character comes from the filter. A paper filter traps coffee oils and very fine particles, while a metal mesh lets a good share of them through. Those oils and fines are what give French press coffee its weight and texture. Handled badly, the same fines turn the cup muddy and gritty, which is why grind and technique matter so much.

Our [French Press](P1) is an immersion brewer made by Fernhill, with a borosilicate glass beaker held in a stainless steel frame [F2, F3, F4, F5]. Its plunger carries a four-layer mesh filter to separate the grounds from the finished coffee [F7].

{{P1}}

## What you need: ratio, dose and batch size

A reliable starting ratio is 1:15 to 1:16 by weight [G]. That works out at roughly 62–67 g of coffee per litre of water [G]. Use the stronger end if you like a dense, syrupy cup and the weaker end for something lighter and easier to drink.

Weigh both the coffee and the water rather than using scoops. Bean size, density and roast level all change how much coffee a scoop holds, so volume measures make it hard to repeat a good brew. A kitchen scale makes the whole process consistent.

Our [French Press](P1) has a capacity of 1 litre and makes about 4 mugs [F1, F6]. You do not have to fill it every time; scale the dose to the water instead:

- 250 ml of water: about 16–17 g of coffee [G].
- 500 ml of water: about 31–33 g of coffee [G].
- 750 ml of water: about 47–50 g of coffee [G].
- 1 litre of water: about 62–67 g of coffee [G].

## Grind coarse and grind fresh

Grind size is the single biggest lever in French press brewing. A coarse grind, roughly like coarse sea salt, slows extraction so the coffee does not turn bitter over a long steep. Just as important, coarse particles are too big to pass through the mesh, so fewer fines end up suspended in your cup.

Evenness matters as much as size. A blade grinder smashes beans into a mix of boulders and dust, and that dust slips straight through the filter. A burr grinder cuts beans to a far more uniform size, which gives a cleaner cup and more predictable extraction. Grind just before you brew, too: ground coffee loses aroma quickly, and the difference is obvious in a method that showcases body and flavour as directly as this one.

Our [Hand Grinder](P2) is a manual grinder with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F11, F12]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, running from espresso at the fine end to French press at the coarse end [F13, F14]. It holds 25 g of beans, so a full-litre batch needs more than one fill [F15]. To compare other options, browse our [grinders](L2).

{{P2}}

## Step by step: brewing your French press

With your coffee weighed and ground, the brew itself is simple. The details below are what separate a clean cup from a muddy one.

- **Preheat the beaker.** Fill it with hot water, swirl, and discard. A warm beaker keeps the brew temperature stable instead of pulling heat out of the water.
- **Add the grounds.** Tip them in and give the beaker a gentle shake to level the bed.
- **Pour water just off the boil.** Aim for roughly 93–96 °C [G]. Without a thermometer, letting a boiled kettle rest for about 30 seconds gets you close [G]. Pour steadily so all the grounds are soaked.
- **Stir gently.** A brief stir makes sure no dry clumps remain. Set the lid on with the plunger pulled all the way up to hold in the heat.
- **Steep.** Leave it for about 4 minutes [G]. A crust of grounds and foam will form on the surface.
- **Break the crust and skim.** Give the crust a gentle stir so most of it sinks, then spoon off the remaining foam and floating grounds. This removes much of the fine material that would otherwise end up in your cup.
- **Let it settle (optional).** For an even cleaner result, wait a few more minutes so the fines drift to the bottom. Extraction slows a lot once the grounds have sunk, so the cup gets clearer rather than harsher.
- **Plunge slowly.** Press the plunger down gently and stop just above the settled grounds. On our [French Press](P1), the four-layer mesh filter does this separating [F7]. Forcing any plunger down fast stirs up the bed and pushes fines through the mesh.
- **Pour it all out at once.** Decant every drop into mugs or a carafe straight away. In an immersion brewer, coffee left sitting on the grounds keeps extracting and turns bitter. Leave the last spoonful in the beaker, where the heaviest sediment collects.

## Choosing beans for the French press

Almost any coffee can be brewed in a French press, but some profiles suit the method especially well. Medium roasts with chocolate and caramel notes sit comfortably with the heavy body of immersion, and the extra texture makes them taste rounder and sweeter. A washed coffee tends to give a clean, sweet base that stays clear even with the oils and fines a mesh filter lets through.

Our [Colombia Huila](P3) fits that profile: it is a washed-process, medium roast coffee with tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F19, F28, F30]. It is a single-origin coffee from Fernhill Roastery and comes in 250 g and 1 kg bags [F21, F22, F23]. You can find more single origins in our [coffee beans](L3) collection.

{{P3}}

### Adjusting the cup

Once you have a baseline, taste and adjust. Change one thing at a time so you know what made the difference.

| What you taste | Likely cause | What to change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sour, thin, sharp | Under-extraction | Grind a little finer or steep a little longer |
| Bitter, dry, harsh | Over-extraction | Grind a little coarser or steep a little shorter |
| Muddy, gritty | Too many fines | Grind coarser, skim the crust, plunge more slowly |
| Weak but balanced | Dose too low | Use more coffee for the same water |

## Cleaning and care

A French press stays good only if it stays clean. Tip spent grounds into the compost or the bin rather than the sink, where they build up in pipes. Rinse the mesh filter under running water after every brew so grounds do not dry into it.

All parts of our [French Press](P1) come apart for cleaning [F8]. Take the plunger and filter fully apart regularly and wash each piece in warm, soapy water. Coffee oils trapped between the mesh layers turn rancid over time and give later brews a stale, bitter edge, even when the press looks clean from the outside.

The borosilicate glass beaker of our [French Press](P1) is also replaceable if it ever breaks [F4, F9].

## Beyond hot brew: cold brew by immersion

The same immersion principle works with cold water. Coarse coffee steeped for many hours in the fridge produces a smooth, low-acidity concentrate that you dilute to taste. You can do this in a French press, but it ties up your brewer and only makes a modest batch.

Our [Cold Brew Jar](P5) is an immersion brewer that makes 1.5 litres of concentrate, with a recommended steep of 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F43, F48, F51]. It has an airtight lid and fits in a fridge door, which makes it the more convenient choice if you keep cold brew on hand regularly [F49, F50]. See the full range in our [immersion brewers](L4) collection.

Whichever way you brew, the fundamentals carry over: weigh your coffee, grind coarse and even, control your time, and separate the coffee from the grounds as soon as it is ready.

Control those variables and you get the heavy, rounded body the method is known for, without sludge at the bottom of the mug. The rest of this guide explains each step, how to read the cup and the plunger to fix problems, and how to keep your press clean.

## Why the French press tastes the way it does

A French press is an immersion brewer. Water does not flow through a bed of coffee, as it does in [pour-over brewing](L1). All of the grounds sit in all of the water for the whole brew. {{P1}}

Weigh both the coffee and the water rather than using scoops or the markings on the beaker. Bean size, density and roast level all change how much coffee a scoop holds, so volume measures make a good brew hard to repeat. A kitchen scale turns the French press from guesswork into a method.

Pick a starting ratio, write it down, and change it only once you have tasted the result. A denser ratio gives a heavier, more syrupy cup; a more dilute one gives a lighter cup that is easier to drink in quantity. Keeping a short brew log of dose, water, grind setting and steep time is the fastest way to find your own recipe and to recover it after switching beans.

Our [French Press](P1) has a capacity of 1 litre and makes about 4 mugs [F1, F6]. You do not have to fill it every time. Keep the ratio fixed and scale the coffee to the amount of water you actually want, so a small morning brew tastes like a full pot.

## Grind coarse, even and fresh

Grind size is the biggest lever in French press brewing. A coarse grind, roughly like coarse sea salt, slows extraction so the coffee does not turn bitter over a long steep. Coarse particles are also too large to pass through the mesh, so fewer fines end up suspended in the cup.

Evenness matters as much as size. A blade grinder smashes beans into a mix of boulders and dust, and that dust slips straight through any mesh filter. The boulders under-extract while the dust over-extracts, so the cup can taste sour and bitter at once. A burr grinder cuts beans to a far more uniform size, which gives a cleaner cup and more predictable extraction. Grind just before brewing as well: ground coffee loses aroma quickly, and a method that shows body and flavour this directly makes stale coffee obvious.

Our [Hand Grinder](P2) is a manual grinder with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F11, F12]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, running from espresso to French press [F13, F14]. It holds 25 g of beans, so check that figure against your dose before you start [F15]. Because the adjustment clicks, you can record the exact setting in your brew log and return to it.

{{P2}}

For buyers who want finer control, our [Electric Flat-Burr Grinder](P6) has 64 mm flat steel burrs and stepless adjustment [F52, F53]. It is a single-dose design with retention under 0.1 g, and bellows on top to puff out remaining grounds [F54, F55, F57]. Compare both options in our [grinders](L2) collection.

## Step by step: brewing your French press

With the coffee weighed and ground, the brew itself is simple. These details separate a clean cup from a muddy one.

- **Preheat the beaker.** Fill it with hot water, swirl and discard. Glass draws heat out of the brew water, and a warm beaker keeps the temperature steadier through the steep.
- **Add the grounds.** Tip them in and give the beaker a gentle shake to level the bed.
- **Pour water just off the boil.** Let the kettle settle briefly after boiling rather than pouring at a rolling boil. Pour steadily so all the grounds are soaked, and put the beaker on the scale so you hit your water weight exactly.
- **Stir gently.** A brief stir makes sure no dry clumps remain. Set the lid on with the plunger pulled all the way up to hold in the heat.
- **Steep.** Start a timer and leave the coffee undisturbed for a few minutes. A crust of grounds and foam forms on the surface. Note the time in your log so you can repeat or adjust it.
- **Break the crust and skim.** Stir the crust gently so most of it sinks, then spoon off the remaining foam and floating grounds. This removes much of the fine material that would otherwise end up in the cup.
- **Let it settle (optional).** For an even cleaner result, wait a few more minutes so the fines drift to the bottom. Extraction slows sharply once the grounds have sunk, so the cup gets clearer rather than harsher.
- **Plunge slowly.** Press the plunger down gently and stop just above the settled grounds. Think of the plunge as a final skimming pass rather than a squeeze. Our [French Press](P1) separates the grounds with its four-layer mesh filter [F7]. Forcing any plunger down fast stirs up the bed and pushes fines through the mesh.
- **Pour it all out at once.** Decant every drop into mugs or a carafe straight away. Coffee left sitting on the grounds keeps extracting and turns bitter. Leave the last spoonful in the beaker, where the heaviest sediment collects.

### Read the plunger

The plunger tells you something about your grind. If it takes real force to push down, the grind is probably too fine and the bed is clogging the mesh; go coarser next time rather than pushing harder. If it drops with almost no resistance and the cup tastes thin, the grind may be too coarse for your steep time.

Almost any coffee works in a French press, but some profiles suit the method especially well. Medium roasts with chocolate and caramel notes sit comfortably with the heavy body of immersion, and the extra texture makes them taste rounder and sweeter. Washed coffees tend to give a clean, sweet base that stays clear even with the oils and fines a mesh filter lets through.

Our [Colombia Huila](P3) fits that profile: it is a washed-process, medium roast coffee with tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F19, F28, F30]. It is a single-origin coffee from Fernhill Roastery and comes in 250 g and 1 kg bags [F21, F22, F23].

{{P3}}

If you want a contrasting cup, our [Ethiopia Guji](P4) is a natural-process, light roast coffee with tasting notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F39, F40, F41]. It is available as whole bean, filter grind or espresso grind, so whole bean is the option to choose if you want to grind coarse for the press yourself [F34]. You can find more single origins in our [coffee beans](L3) collection.

Once you have a baseline, taste and adjust. Change one variable at a time so you know what made the difference, and taste the cup again as it cools, when flaws show more clearly.

| What you taste | Likely cause | What to change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sour, thin, sharp | Under-extraction | Grind a little finer or steep a little longer |
| Bitter, dry, harsh | Over-extraction | Grind a little coarser or steep a little shorter |
| Muddy, gritty | Too many fines | Grind coarser, skim the crust, let it settle, plunge more slowly |
| Weak but balanced | Dose too low | Use more coffee for the same water |
| Sour and bitter together | Uneven grind | Use a burr grinder and grind just before brewing |

A French press only keeps brewing well if it stays clean. Tip spent grounds into the compost or the bin rather than the sink, where they build up in pipes. Rinse the mesh filter under running water after every brew so grounds do not dry into it.
